passage:
School counsellor's note. Nikita ma'am, Friday.
Gautam, Class 11, came to see me after a classmate reported he was collecting money from friends. He explained that a popular dancer he follows online, "the best dancer in the country," had posted about a trading scheme that "doubles your pocket money in a week". He had put in two thousand rupees and wanted to put in more. When I asked what he knew about the scheme, he said, "Nothing, but he wouldn't lie. He's so talented." He was proud and excited, not secretive.
What I did: I didn't mock him. We looked together at what the dancer is actually expert in, and I asked him to show the scheme to his parents today. I also informed his class teacher.

qa.q: How much had Gautam put in?
qa.a: Gautam had put in two thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why does Gautam feel the dancer wouldn't lie?
qa.a: He admires the dancer's talent so much that the admiration spills over into trusting the dancer about money too, where the dancer has no special knowledge.

qa.q: Why were the counsellor's steps sensible?
qa.a: Not mocking kept Gautam talking, separating the dancer's real skill from money claims helped him think, and involving his parents the same day protects him from losing more.

qa.q: How might the friends who gave Gautam money be affected?
qa.a: They could lose their pocket money too, since they trusted Gautam's excitement, which itself came from trusting the dancer.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy believing a talented online dancer about a money scheme because admiration for the dancing carries over to everything.

passage:
Thursday
The singer I follow, the one with the most amazing voice, posted a video today about a herbal drink that "stops you ever getting sick". She looks so healthy and glowing, and her songs are the best, so it must work, right? I asked Mummy to order it. She said we'll ask Dr. Nirmala at the clinic first. I got annoyed. Why would a singer that famous lie? Then Pema said her cousin tried it and got a stomach ache. I said that's probably a fake story. But now I'm lying here wondering: the singer is great at singing. Is she great at medicine too? I never thought about it like that.
Tenzin

qa.q: What did the singer's video say the herbal drink does?
qa.a: The video said it stops you ever getting sick.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin feel the drink must work?
qa.a: Tenzin admires the singer's voice and glowing look, and that admiration spreads to believing the singer about health too.

qa.q: What was wise about Mummy's reply, and what could Tenzin add?
qa.a: Asking Dr. Nirmala first checks the claim with someone trained in health; Tenzin could keep asking the new question: what is this person really expert in?

qa.q: How might Dr. Nirmala respond when asked about the drink?
qa.a: Dr. Nirmala would likely look at the claim calmly and explain that big health promises need checking by someone trained, whoever makes them.

grounding: Shows a teenager believing a talented, good-looking singer about a health product because admiration for one area carries over to all.

passage:
In their kasba near Bikaner, Jyoti and her cousin Rehana watched stunt-rider videos on Rehana's phone every evening on the roof. The rider was handsome, fearless and could stand on a moving bike. Last week he started a new series: "Join my Lucky Circle for 500 rupees. Bring three friends, and your money doubles in a month."
Jyoti counted her savings from the tin under her bed. "He can do anything on a bike," she said. "He wouldn't lie to his fans."
Rehana scrolled back. "He's brilliant at riding. What does riding have to do with money?"
Jyoti opened her mouth, then shut it. She'd never asked that. Everything about him had just seemed good at once.
"Let's ask Bua," Rehana said. "She keeps the accounts for the women's group."
Jyoti put the tin back under her bed, still unsure, and went downstairs with Rehana to find Bua.

qa.q: How much money did the rider ask people to pay to join the Lucky Circle?
qa.a: He asked for 500 rupees.

qa.q: Why did it feel reasonable to Jyoti to trust the rider about money?
qa.a: She admired his fearless riding so much that everything about him seemed good at once, so she believed he would not lie to his fans about money either.

qa.q: What turning point stopped Jyoti from paying straight away?
qa.a: Rehana's question about what riding has to do with money made Jyoti see she had never asked, and she chose to check with Bua, who keeps the women's group accounts, before doing anything.

qa.q: How might Rehana see the rider after that evening?
qa.a: Rehana still thinks he is brilliant at riding but now looks at his money claims separately, and may feel protective of Jyoti's savings in the tin.

grounding: It shows a teenager trusting an admired, talented online figure about money because admiration in one area spreads to everything, and a trusted adult being brought in.

passage:
Dalia had a sore throat that had been scratching for a while. At dinner in their Leeds flat she kept quiet about it. Instead, she sprayed a little bottle of herbal throat mist she had ordered after watching Kiana, a skateboarder with perfect curls and a million followers. In one video Kiana had landed a trick and then said, "With this spray, I never need a doctor."
Her older brother Siddiq noticed the bottle. "Since when do you trust sprays from the internet?"
"She's amazing, Siddiq. She's so healthy. She wouldn't sell something useless."
"She's amazing on a board," he said. "Does she know anything about throats?"
Dalia paused. She had never thought about that. Kiana's skill, her looks, her confidence, all of it had blended into "she knows best."
"Tell Dad about your throat," Siddiq said. "If it keeps going or worries you, check with the doctor."
Dalia pushed the bottle aside and nodded.

qa.q: What did Kiana say in the video after landing a trick?
qa.a: She said, "With this spray, I never need a doctor."

qa.q: Why did Kiana's words about the spray feel believable to Dalia?
qa.a: Dalia admired Kiana's skill, looks and confidence so much that they blended into a feeling that she knows best, even about health.

qa.q: What was the key choice at the end of the scene, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Dalia agreed to tell Dad about her throat instead of relying on the spray, so a trusted adult and, if needed, a doctor could look at it.

qa.q: How might Siddiq feel when he spots the bottle?
qa.a: Siddiq seems a bit worried about his sister hiding her sore throat, and wants to separate how good Kiana is on a board from whether she knows anything about throats.

grounding: It shows a teenager trusting a skilled, good-looking online figure about health because admiration in one area carries over, and turning to a trusted adult.

Monday. Mridul's favourite gamer, the one who could clear any level blindfolded, posted a video: "Stop wasting pocket money! This app doubled mine in a week." Mridul watched it five times. "He's a genius," he told Tenzin. "If he says it works, it works."
Wednesday. Mridul downloaded the app. It wanted a deposit and his father's card details. Tenzin read the fine print over his shoulder. "Bro, he's good at games. Not at money. And look, it's a paid promotion." Mridul frowned. "He wouldn't lie to us."
Saturday. Mridul showed his father the app before entering anything. His father searched the app's name with the word "complaints" and found pages of people who had lost money. Mridul deleted it and sat very still. "I trusted him because he's good at games," he said slowly. "That's not the same thing."

qa.q: What did the app ask for on Wednesday?
qa.a: A deposit and his father's card details.

qa.q: Why did Mridul trust the gamer about money?
qa.a: He admired the gamer's skill so much that the glow spread to everything, so a money claim felt as trustworthy as a gaming tip.

qa.q: What went right on Saturday?
qa.a: Mridul showed his father before entering anything, and together they found the complaints before any money was lost.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see the gamer's video?
qa.a: Tenzin sees a paid promotion from someone good at games but not at money, and tries to warn Mridul.

grounding: Over a week, a teenage boy nearly trusts a gamer's money claim because he admires the gamer's skill, until his father helps him check.

passage: Kishore, you think that fitness star knows everything because he's handsome and famous? Sit. Let your Yusuf uncle tell you something. At fifteen, my hero was a film actor with perfect hair and a smile on every poster in Hyderabad. When he said on TV that a certain tonic made him strong and sharp, I spent my whole Eid money on three bottles. I drank it every morning before school and felt exactly the same, only poorer. My ammi asked the pharmacist, who laughed kindly and said, "It's mostly sugar syrup." I was so angry, not at the actor, at myself. He was a good actor. That was all he had ever shown me. After that, I asked one question about every famous face: good at what, exactly?

qa.q: What did young Yusuf spend his Eid money on?
qa.a: Three bottles of the tonic.

qa.q: Why was young Yusuf so angry at himself after the pharmacist spoke?
qa.a: He felt foolish and angry, realising he had trusted the actor about health only because he admired his looks and acting.

qa.q: What question did Yusuf start asking, and why is it useful?
qa.a: "Good at what, exactly?" It separates the skill someone really has from everything else they claim.

qa.q: How might the pharmacist have seen young Yusuf's bottles?
qa.a: The pharmacist seemed kind and a little amused, knowing the tonic was mostly sugar syrup and not wanting to embarrass the boy.

grounding: An uncle recalls how, at fifteen, admiration for a handsome actor made him believe the actor's health claim about a tonic.

passage: Exam week, and Keerthana had no time to think. So when the dancer she had followed for two years, the one who could spin six times on one foot, posted a video holding a jar of green powder, Keerthana believed every word. "I skip lunch and just drink this. Energy for hours!" The dancer's skin glowed, her smile was perfect, her routines flawless. Surely she knew about energy too. Keerthana ordered a jar with her birthday money and skipped lunch on Monday. By the second paper on Wednesday her head felt light and her hands shook. The school nurse gave her a banana and said she should eat proper meals and ask a doctor before trying any powder. Trisha, walking her back to class, asked quietly, "Why did you trust her about food? She's a dancer." Keerthana had no answer.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana believe the dancer so completely?
qa.a: Keerthana admired the dancer's flawless routines and glowing looks, so it felt safe and natural to trust her about food as well.

qa.q: What would be a wiser step when an admired person gives health tips?
qa.a: Ask whether that person actually knows about health, and check with a doctor or the school nurse before trying anything.

qa.q: Why might Trisha see the dancer differently from Keerthana?
qa.a: Trisha separates the dancer's talent from her knowledge, seeing a skilled dancer, not an expert on food.

grounding: Shows a teenager trusting a talented, good-looking dancer about food because admiration for one skill spreads to everything.

passage:
I'm Kavitha. In Class 10, there was a dancer online I loved. She had millions of followers, amazing moves, perfect hair. I watched every video.

Then she started posting about a "detox tea" that she said cleared skin and gave energy. She was so talented and beautiful that I believed it straight away. I asked Amma for money to buy it.

Amma asked, "Is she a doctor?"

I said no, but she's so good at dancing.

Amma said, "Being good at dancing doesn't make her good at health. Let's ask Dr Menon next time we see her."

My sister Lavanya laughed at me a bit. But when we asked the doctor, she said the tea had no proof behind it and could upset the stomach.

I still love the dancer's videos. But I realised I'd believed her about tea just because she dances well. Now I ask: is this person actually an expert in this?

qa.q: What did the dancer say the detox tea did?
qa.a: She said it cleared skin and gave energy.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha believe the dancer about the tea?
qa.a: Kavitha felt such admiration for the dancer's talent and looks that it spread to trusting her about health, even though she wasn't a doctor.

qa.q: What question does Kavitha now ask, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Kavitha asks whether the person is actually an expert in the topic, which stops admiration in one area from carrying over to everything.

qa.q: How did Amma handle Kavitha's request?
qa.a: Amma calmly asked if the dancer was a doctor and suggested checking with Dr Menon, turning the moment into a lesson rather than a scolding.

grounding: A teenager believes a talented, good-looking dancer's claim about a health tea because admiration carries over, until a doctor is asked.

passage:
Maths teacher's note, Class 11

Vijay came to me after class today, very excited. A cricketer he follows online had posted that "anyone can double their money in a month" by playing on a fantasy-sports app. Vijay said he was going to put his birthday money in.

I asked why he trusted this. He said, "He's the best batsman in the state. He knows what he's talking about." When I asked what the cricketer knows about money, Vijay paused.

We talked about how being brilliant at cricket doesn't make someone an expert in money. I didn't give him money advice; that isn't my role. I told him to talk to his parents before doing anything and suggested he ask who pays the cricketer to post.

He looked at the post again. It said "sponsored" in small letters. He was quiet.

I've let his class teacher know so his parents can be told today.

Hafsa

qa.q: What did the cricketer say anyone could do?
qa.a: Anyone can double their money in a month.

qa.q: Why did Vijay trust the cricketer's money claim?
qa.a: Vijay felt such admiration for the cricketer's batting that it spread to trusting him about money, though he had no expertise there.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do that was wise?
qa.a: Hafsa asked what the cricketer knows about money, pointed Vijay to his parents rather than giving advice, and informed the class teacher the same day.

qa.q: How might Vijay's parents feel when they hear about this?
qa.a: Vijay's parents may feel worried but grateful the teacher caught it before he spent his birthday money.

grounding: A teacher notes a teenager who trusts a star cricketer's money claim because admiration for his batting carries over.

passage:
Saturday

Almost spent all my savings today on a hair serum. Writing this to remember why I didn't.

Riya Rao, the singer I love, posted about it. "My secret to thick hair!" Her voice is amazing, and her hair is gorgeous, and I thought, if she says it, it must work. I had the order page open.

Then I messaged Sachin, who always asks annoying questions. He said, "Is she a doctor? Or is she paid to say it?"

I checked. The post said "paid partnership" at the top.

And no, she's not a doctor. She's a singer. A brilliant one. But being brilliant at singing doesn't mean she knows about hair medicine.

I felt a bit stupid, honestly. I'd trusted her about everything because I admire her voice.

Closed the order page. If I'm worried about my hair, I'll ask Amma to take me to a doctor.

Kavitha

qa.q: What did the post say at the top?
qa.a: The post said "paid partnership" at the top.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha nearly buy the serum?
qa.a: Kavitha felt such admiration for Riya Rao's voice and looks that it carried over to trusting her about hair products.

qa.q: What did Sachin's questions do that helped?
qa.a: Sachin asked whether the singer was a doctor or paid, which made Kavitha check and see the admiration was spilling into a topic the singer isn't expert in.

qa.q: How might Amma respond if Kavitha asks to see a doctor about her hair?
qa.a: Amma would probably feel glad Kavitha asked and help arrange it, rather than Kavitha buying something from a post.

grounding: A teenager nearly buys a hair product because admiration for a singer carries over to trusting her about health.
